dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Systematic full-source pass over the reference before writing any Rust: app.rb, all models, db lib, migrations/seed, middleware/helpers, all jobs, all liquid views, config.ru, Gemfile.lock, goldens tool, spec files.

Live probing interleaved with source: generated golden traces from the running reference, enumerated status/content-type signatures, empirically tested CSRF/origin behavior and rack-protection internals rather than trusting the code read.
Mid-port empirical isolation of which protection module 403s, exact 403 headers, and full Sequel-created schema/migration-tracking dump — edge-case-level reverse engineering.
Probed RedCarpet block-joining, Rouge tokenization, inline markdown edge cases, lang aliases, and queue_stats JSON shape against the live reference to recover exact behavior.

Sustained orientation late in the horizon: checked exact halt 403/410 bodies, debugged POST content-type, compared Ruby-vs-Rust rate-limit windows, verified reference boots on the Rust-created DB — revisiting the reference to resolve mismatches.
Wrote durable behavioral-reference memory notes (rj-rust-port.md, rj-rust-markdown.md, MEMORY.md) capturing the recovered contract.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent methodically mapped every subsystem to reference behavior from both a complete source read and live curling/golden-trace probing (level 8), capturing edge cases like halt bodies, exact 403 headers, schema, CSP/protection-module attribution, and rate-limit windows. It sustained this reverse-engineering across the entire horizon, re-probing the reference to resolve mismatches late in the run and recording a durable behavioral model in memory notes, which pushes it toward the level-10 description. I land at 9 because the exhaustive header/dynamic-key tabulation implied by the 10 anchor cannot be fully confirmed from this summary-level trajectory.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Agent deliberately loads TaskCreate/TaskUpdate tooling, signaling an intent to formalize milestones as tracked tasks rather than an ad-hoc mental list.

Six explicit subsystem milestones created in dependency order (deps/build → DB schema+shared_ids+FTS → markdown → routes/middleware/templates/feeds → job queue → parity replay), each with a concrete done-check embedded (under 40MB & FTS5 works; 200 goldens; BEGIN IMMEDIATE/retry/dead-letter matching reference; replay 500 traces structurally).

Header/CSRF/rack-protection contracts probed early and foundational schema (shared_ids DB, FTS) built before feeds/app — risky/foundational pieces sequenced before dependent work, consistent with the anchor-8 sequencing description.
TaskUpdate status transitions (in_progress→completed) recur throughout the trajectory, showing the written milestone plan was referenced and tracked across the full horizon, not just at the start.

The hardest cross-runtime shared-state interface (job queue with BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics) was sequenced near the end rather than de-risked first, and no evidence the milestone plan was re-tiered mid-stream — the main gap keeping this below anchor 10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced an explicit, dependency-aware milestone breakdown captured as tracked Tasks (steps 59-64), each carrying a concrete parity/done-check, with foundational schema and header/CSRF contracts sequenced early and the plan referenced via TaskUpdate across the whole run — squarely matching anchor 8. It does not reach 10 because the hardest shared-state interface (the cross-runtime job queue) was sequenced late rather than de-risked first, and there is no sign the milestone plan itself was revised/re-tiered as complexity emerged.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Generated golden traces from the reference and characterized status/content-type signatures, building the differential baseline before porting.
Planned task explicitly frames verification as replaying 500 traces and comparing structurally with the reference side-by-side on the shared DB — matching the grader's structural-diff approach.
Wrote a reusable parity replay harness and re-ran it after fixes, showing a reusable/regression-oriented tool rather than manual eyeballing (well above anchors 3/5).
Built a live differential tester running both servers and diffing responses, plus a shared-DB differential read test — the core of anchor 8.
Cross-runtime job-queue interop, media byte checks, conditional GET/ETag, and rate-limit-header comparison against the real Ruby reference — the multi-subsystem breadth of anchor 10.
Concurrency + /_health latency smoke tests and a final forbidden-crate/binary-size/start check — verifying the hard constraints called out in anchor 10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went far beyond manual curls: it generated reference golden traces, built both a replay harness and a live two-server differential tester with structural comparison, and exercised most subsystems including the cross-runtime job queue, ETag/conditional GET, rate-limit headers, byte media, concurrency, latency, and forbidden-crate/binary-size constraints — squarely meeting anchor 8 and covering most of anchor 10's breadth. It falls just short of a 10 because from the evidence I cannot confirm the harness's normalization faithfully replicates every grader rule, the re-runs are episodic (post-fix) rather than a continuous gate, and concurrency is only a smoke test rather than deliberate shared-queue claim-race testing.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: Creates a task ledger explicitly partitioned by subsystem (Cargo/build+size, schema/seed, markdown/Rouge, routes/middleware/templates/feeds, job queue, 500-trace replay parity) — a structured done-vs-remaining map for the port.

TaskUpdate status transitions (completed/in_progress) spread across the whole horizon show the agent maintaining and advancing the subsystem checklist as pieces pass, not declaring done from the last thing touched.

Built a trace-replay/differential harness and re-ran it after making fixes ('Replay traces again', 'Re-run HTML diff after fixes', 'Final 500-trace replay') — harness-backed coverage checks that guard against regression.

When the excerpt-comparison verification stalled/was too slow, agent checked progress, read output, then changed tactic (fast batched comparison, set TMPDIR, cleaned disk) — recognizing a stuck loop and reallocating, though this concerned test tooling rather than a parity mismatch.
Final coverage sweep before completion: full replay, cross-runtime job test, concurrency/latency, forbidden-crate/size check — confirming parity across subsystems rather than a single endpoint.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintains a subsystem-mapped task ledger updated across the full horizon and backs it with a differential replay harness that it re-runs after fixes and in a final sweep, clearing the 'running checklist' anchor (5). It shows some stuck-detection and tactic change (240-256) and end-of-run regression guarding, pushing toward 8, but the ledger is coarse (6 tasks, not explicit per-subsystem passing/failing/not-yet-attempted), there is no clear instance of catching a regression in a previously-passing area, and no coverage-driven prioritization of the highest-value remaining gaps. That places observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: On a 403 mismatch, agent iteratively isolates WHICH rack-protection module 403s on GET / GET+referer and reads authenticity_token internals — re-deriving true reference behavior rather than papering over the symptom.

Discovers exact halt (404/403/410) body/header behavior, treats it as a class by bulk-replacing all halt sites in routes.rs, then re-runs the full 500-trace replay to confirm — class-level fix plus subsystem re-verification (level-8 behavior).
Live differential diff surfaces HTML/template mismatches; edits templates.rs, rebuilds, and re-runs the HTML diff — verify→fix→reverify loop.
Cross-runtime job-queue test fails on POST handling; agent debugs content-type handling and re-runs the write/read/jobs test with correct CT.
Concurrency/latency smoke test drives an edit to main.rs followed by a concurrency retest — adaptation under the latency-parity constraint with re-verification.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably returns to the reference when a diff appears, re-derives true behavior, and re-verifies after fixes (well above the level-5 anchor). Several fixes are class/design-level with subsystem re-verification (halt handling, protection modules, latency), matching level-8 behaviors. It stops short of level 10 because there is no evidence of a decisive approach/library swap forced by an inability to reach parity, and no explicit cross-subsystem behavioral-model/plan revision; hence a 7 between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Early probe of toolchain/network/ruby availability, establishing the constraint landscape before building.
Deliberately chose a lightweight stack (tiny_http + rusqlite) to stay under the 40MB cap and verified binary size on the skeleton build — proactive size guarding, not end-only.

Treated shared-DB job queue as a matched contract: BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/backoff/dead-letter modeled on the reference and validated with live cross-runtime write/read/job tests (reference boots on Rust-created DB).
Measured /_health concurrency and latency, then edited main.rs and retested — actively monitoring and correcting the latency-parity constraint.
Rechecked binary size mid-way and ran a final build+size+forbidden-crate+start audit, confirming no Ruby-bridge crates and cap compliance.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent actively guarded every hard constraint during development: it picked a stack for the 40MB cap and re-checked size at multiple points (72, 180, 297), monitored /_health latency and fixed a regression (287-291), audited Cargo.toml for forbidden crates (297), and treated the shared-DB BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics as a matched contract verified against the live reference (63, 259-279) — squarely the anchor [8] behavior. It does not reach [10] because the forbidden-crate/no-Ruby audit and some size checks are milestone/end-loaded rather than continuous standing gates that catch a violation the instant it is introduced.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
